_about: Action tracks people can add next to the basic learning path. Steps are practical habits, not courses, so they carry no numbers about jobs or pay. 'examples' tailor a step to a career family; families group the 20 careers. Links were checked to respond on 2026-10-22; local links apply only to the country named.

tracks.title: LinkedIn & personal brand
tracks.about: Let employers find you and see what you are learning.

steps.title: Add a clear photo and a headline
steps.why: A headline that names the job you want tells recruiters what to search you for.
how: Use a plain, friendly photo of your face.
Write a headline with the role you are moving into and 2–3 skills, e.g. "Aspiring {role} · {skills}".

links.label: LinkedIn Help: create a good profile

steps.title: Write your About section
steps.why: Three short paragraphs explain your story better than a list of past jobs.
how: Where you are now and what you are good at.
Why you are moving towards {role}.
What you are learning right now (name the course from your path).

steps.title: List the skills from your plan
steps.why: Recruiters filter by skills, so use the same words employers use.
how: Add the skills you already have from your profile here.
Add each new skill when you mark its step done on your path.

steps.title: Post about your first finished step
steps.why: A short post shows you follow through. It also gives people something to react to.
how: Say what you learned in 3–4 sentences and one thing you will try at work.
Add the course certificate or a screenshot if there is one.

examples.tech: Share a small chart or query you made while practising.
examples.marketing: Share a before/after of a post or page you improved.
examples.health: Share what you learned about records or lab safety, never patient details.
examples.lab: Share a technique you practised, never unpublished results.
examples.farming: Share a photo of a field practice you tried and what changed.
examples.green: Share a simple energy or waste saving you measured.
examples.making: Share a process fix or checklist you made.
examples.office: Share a template or workflow that saved you time.

steps.title: Post once a week for a month
steps.why: Regular short posts keep your name in front of people in your field.
how: Pick one day a week.
Rotate: something you learned, a useful link with your own comment, a question to your network.
Tick this step after four weeks in a row.

steps.title: Comment thoughtfully on others' posts
steps.why: Good comments start conversations with people already working as {role}.
how: Follow 10 people or companies in your field.
Each week, add a real comment to 2–3 of their posts: a question or your own experience.

steps.title: Add a Featured project
steps.why: One concrete piece of work is stronger than any claim.
how: Pin your best project, post or certificate to the Featured section.

examples.tech: A dashboard or script on GitHub.
examples.health: A records clean-up or process you improved (no patient data).
examples.lab: A poster or write-up of a technique.
examples.farming: A field trial log or photo series.
examples.green: An energy or carbon calculation you did.
examples.making: A quality checklist or before/after defect count.

steps.title: Turn on "Open to work" for {role}
steps.why: Recruiters can then see the roles and places you want.
how: Choose who can see it (all members or recruiters only).
Add {role} and nearby job titles.

tracks.title: Real experience
tracks.about: Use your skills on real work before you apply: internships, volunteering, projects.

steps.title: Search for internships, attachments or trainee roles
steps.why: Short placements count as experience on your resume.
how: Search for "{role}" plus "intern", "trainee" or "attachment".
Save 5 that fit your hours and location.

examples.health: Hospitals and clinics often run attachments for records and lab staff.
examples.lab: University and hospital labs take short-term lab assistants.
examples.farming: Farms, plantations and agricultural institutes offer field attachments.
examples.green: Solar installers and energy consultancies take trainees.
examples.making: Factories run apprenticeship and technician trainee schemes.

steps.title: Volunteer with your new skills
steps.why: Volunteering gives real tasks, references and stories for interviews.
how: Offer one skill from your path to a charity, community group or small business.

examples.tech: Clean up a spreadsheet or set up basic security for a small group.
examples.marketing: Run social media for a community group for a month.
examples.health: Help at health screenings or blood drives.
examples.office: Organise schedules or records for a community group.
examples.green: Help a community group measure its energy or waste.

steps.title: Do one small project end to end
steps.why: A finished project shows you can do the job, not just pass a course.
how: Pick a real problem you can finish in 2–4 weeks.
Write down the problem, what you did and the result.

examples.tech: Analyse a public dataset and share the notebook.
examples.marketing: Grow a small page or newsletter and report what worked.
examples.health: Design a cleaner records checklist for a clinic workflow (no real patient data).
examples.lab: Write up a standard procedure for a technique you practised.
examples.farming: Keep a season log for one plot: inputs, weather, yield.
examples.green: Do an energy walk-through of a home or office and list savings.
examples.making: Map a process step and cut one source of defects.
examples.office: Automate one weekly task and time the saving.

steps.title: Shadow someone doing {role} for a day
steps.why: You see the real daily work and meet someone who can refer you.
how: Ask a contact (see the Networking track) if you can join them for a few hours.

steps.title: Ask for a reference or recommendation
steps.why: Someone else vouching for your work carries weight with employers.
how: Ask your supervisor or volunteer lead for a short LinkedIn recommendation or a reference letter.

steps.title: Add the experience to your resume
steps.why: Your resume page can then show it next to your finished skills.
how: Write one line per placement: what you did, with which skill, and the result.
Add it under Experience in the Resume page.

tracks.title: Networking
tracks.about: Meet people already doing the job. Many roles are filled through referrals.

steps.title: Join one professional group or community
steps.why: Groups share openings, events and advice before they are public.
how: Find one online group and one local meetup for {role}.

examples.tech: A local data, cloud or security meetup.
examples.marketing: A digital marketing or content creators' group.
examples.health: A health informatics or medical lab professionals' group.
examples.lab: A university or industry lab users' group.
examples.farming: A farmers' association or agri-tech community.
examples.green: A renewable energy or sustainability professionals' network.
examples.making: A manufacturing, automation or quality group.
examples.office: An admin professionals' or HR community.

steps.title: Go to one event and talk to two people
steps.why: Short, real conversations are how people remember you.
how: Prepare one line about yourself and one question to ask.
Connect on LinkedIn the same day with a short note.

chapters.title: Learn from people in the job

steps.title: Ask for a 20-minute chat with someone in {role}
steps.why: An informational interview tells you what the job is really like and who is hiring.
how: Ask politely, say why you chose them, keep it short.
Prepare 3–5 questions: their day, the skills that matter, how they got in.

steps.title: Follow up and stay in touch
steps.why: A thank-you and a later update turn a chat into a contact.
how: Send thanks within a day.
Tell them a month later what you did with their advice.

steps.title: Practise speaking in front of others
steps.why: Confidence in meetings and interviews is part of most jobs.
how: Join a speaking club or offer a short talk at work or in your group.

steps.title: Help someone newer than you
steps.why: Sharing what you know builds your reputation and deepens your own skills.
how: Answer a question in your group or mentor a newcomer for an hour.

tracks.title: Job hunting
tracks.about: Turn your new skills into applications and interviews.

steps.title: Tailor your resume to {role}
steps.why: A resume that uses the job's own words passes screening more often.
how: Open your Resume page.
Match your skills list and summary to the words in 3 real job ads.

steps.title: Make a list of 10 target employers
steps.why: A short list helps you follow companies closely instead of applying everywhere.
how: Include large and small employers near you.
Follow them on LinkedIn and note who hires for {role}.

steps.title: Apply to a few good matches each week
steps.why: A steady pace of careful applications beats many rushed ones.
how: Pick 3 a week that fit well.
Write two lines on why you fit each one.
Tick this step after a month of applying.

steps.title: Keep a simple application log
steps.why: Knowing where you applied and when to follow up stops chances slipping away.
how: Note company, role, date, contact and next step.
Follow up politely after about a week.

steps.title: Prepare three work stories
steps.why: Interviewers ask for examples: what happened, what you did and the result.
how: One about a problem you solved.
One about working with others.
One about learning something new fast (your path counts).

steps.title: Do a practice interview
steps.why: Saying answers out loud once makes the real interview far easier.
how: Ask a friend, a contact or a career centre to run a 30-minute mock interview.
Ask for one thing to improve.
